review:
Bayonetta is a fun, stylish slasher that clearly shares DNA with Devil May Cry and, surprisingly, Ōkami. Its core combat is excellent, but a handful of design problems keep it from reaching greatness. That sounds harsh for a game I had fun with and genuinely wanted to love, especially since I already admired Clover Studios/Platinum’s Ōkami and God Hand. Bayonetta absolutely oozes style, but for me it has too many issues to fully enjoy.

Combat: Bayonetta’s moment-to-moment combat is very good. The weapon system is creative, with different weapons for hands and legs that each have unique combos and can chain into one another in interesting ways. Unlockable moves and advanced mechanics add real depth. My issue is that many basic damage strings may look different, but they often serve the same purpose, which makes some of them feel redundant. It is not that they are hard to learn; it is that there are so many of them, yet when you have a damage window there is often not much reason to choose one over another. You could argue this is pure skill expression, and that is fair, but once you reach higher difficulties a lot of those options are functionally outclassed anyway. Enemies get faster, tankier, and more defensive, so the safest and most efficient routes dominate. In practice, Wicked Weaves also overshadow regular combos in damage, recovery, and area control.

Bosses: Bosses have some cool set pieces and strong introductions, but most of them feel more like oversized regular enemies than memorable bespoke encounters. They usually do not require especially distinct strategies and can often be handled like standard foes. The game also leans on reusing “important” enemies later, which undercuts their uniqueness. By the time I am fighting the same angelic enemy for the fourth time, like Temperance, the novelty is gone.

Jeanne fights: These were the hardest for me to enjoy. Presentation-wise, they are some of the best fights in the game: great music, great set pieces, and huge spectacle. But Jeanne feels like Bayonetta on steroids. She can punish instantly, break out of stuns, parry, and generally ignore the rules the player has to live by. The problem is not just that she is strong; it is that she uses the same toolkit as Bayonetta but with extra privileges. You cannot safely rely on long combos because she can escape them, and she will also parry ranged attacks on sight. To be effective, you almost have to use fast combo strings into Wicked Weaves before she escapes or punishes you. It feels less like a duel and more like fighting someone who is cheating. To be fair, you can eventually unlock items that let you parry and trigger instant Wicked Weaves, but that comes very late and is not something you can just toggle on.

Healing: Healing is tied to rare items you must buy or craft, with very few natural recovery opportunities between fights. That makes the game feel harsh in a way that is not especially fun. You can leave one encounter nearly empty on health and find no meaningful recovery before the next one. Later areas get stingier with breakable objects, which makes this worse. The result is that you are encouraged to stockpile healing items, but ingredients are scarce, so your options are often limited to buying them with Halos or grinding Angel Attack.

QTEs and torture attacks: The instant-death QTEs are a real low point. Early in the game, many QTEs are clear and generously telegraphed, so it is frustrating when later ones become sudden and poorly signposted. The inconsistency is especially annoying because different sequences ask for different inputs, sometimes even different kinds of inputs entirely. Torture Attacks have a similar problem. They all begin with the same activation, but the follow-up QTEs vary, and their damage depends on score, which depends on how many button presses you can cram in under pressure. On higher difficulties this becomes especially obnoxious. It is one thing to have a flashy finisher; it is another to make it feel like a test of whether your hands can survive the button-mashing. Up through Normal, most enemies die to one Torture Attack, but on Hard and Non-stop Infinite Climax it barely moves the health bar.

Camera and targeting: The camera is frequently obstructive, especially when enemies use wide sweeping attacks and slip out of frame. That makes both dodging and targeting harder than they should be. Since so many encounters involve multiple enemies, the constant fight to keep the camera on target becomes a burden. Bayonetta does occasionally use a more fixed perspective, but even then the camera can swing around and become disorienting. Targeting is also awkward. Switching targets mid-combo is unreliable, and the game often chooses a different enemy than the one you meant to hit. Bayonetta will sometimes lock onto something off-screen or swap targets at the worst possible moment.

Halos and scoring: The Halo economy is fine in theory. Like DMC, it uses an in-world currency for items, skills, cosmetics, some weapons, and important upgrades like health and magic. But because performance affects how much currency you earn, a lot of the game’s other problems feed back into one another. Getting hit, dying, using items, or dropping combos all hurt your payout, which means the camera, healing, and QTE issues do not just feel bad in isolation; they also reduce your ability to progress comfortably. The scoring system itself works in a vacuum, but combined with the rest of the game it feels overly punitive.

Story: I like the presentation and the overall style, but the story itself is mediocre. The cast is one-dimensional, and a lot of the storytelling comes through static cutscenes that interrupt the flow more than they enhance it. Some scenes are visually cool, but many are just exposition or repetitive banter. Luka feels more interested in Bayonetta than in his actual goals, and Jeanne is basically trying to be Vergil. Balder is the biggest problem. His plan is to resurrect Jubileus and remake reality, but the game never explains him clearly enough. He speaks in abstractions instead of direct answers. The result is that I had to rewatch cutscenes to understand what he was saying.

The bigger issue is that his plan feels contrived. He mind-controls Jeanne, but apparently cannot find Bayonetta himself and just waits 500 years for her to wake up. Angels kill Luka’s father after he finds Bayonetta, but Luka is inexplicably left alive. Balder knows Bayonetta has lost her memories, yet never seems to use that more directly. He says he orchestrated the event so she gradually recovers her memories and awakens the Left Eye, but it is hard not to wonder whether there was an easier way. The mythic framing may be the intended explanation, but the game never sells it convincingly enough. As it stands, the broad strokes work, but the execution feels clunky.

Mini-games: The pacing also takes a hit from the long mini-game stages. On a first playthrough they are novel enough, but they go on for too long and repeat too often. Chapter 8's bike ride and Chapter 14's Star Fox-style sequences becomes exhausting when stretched across long stretches of near-identical gameplay. Replaying those sections makes the problem much more obvious. At that point I just want to get back to the actual combat.

UI/UX: This is a smaller complaint, but the menu navigation is clunky. Combo lists are hard to find, the close-button behavior is awkward, pickup notifications interrupt the flow too much, and practice mode access feels unnecessarily buried.

Technical note: Since I game on Linux, I should mention that the game ran flawlessly on Arch under Proton 10 with no extra settings. I did not get major performance dips or crashes, even after hours of play.

Final score: 3/5 — Worth playing for the combat, but major design flaws stop it short of excellence.

Bayonetta is often praised as one of the greatest character-action games ever made, and its combat system certainly shows why. However, while the core combat is excellent, I found much of the overall experience surprisingly random.

Pros:

+ Deep and rewarding combat system with a huge range of combos.
+ Witch Time is a fantastic mechanic that makes dodging feel satisfying.
+ Great weapon variety and customization options.
+ Epic boss battles with impressive scale.
+ Smooth performance and excellent PC optimization.
+ Strong replay value for players who enjoy mastering the combat.

Cons:

- Story feels random, confusing, and difficult to follow.
- Gameplay frequently shifts between different mechanics and gimmicks.
- Vehicle sections, shooting segments, and other mini-games feel disconnected from the core experience.
- The game often prioritizes spectacle over consistency.
- Over-the-top presentation can become exhausting after a while.
- Camera can be frustrating during chaotic encounters.
- QTEs are outdated and can lead to unfair deaths.

Bayonetta's combat is undeniably excellent, but the game constantly jumps between different gameplay styles, throws in unexpected gimmicks, and tells a story that rarely feels grounded or coherent. While action-game enthusiasts may appreciate the variety and spectacle, I found the experience inconsistent and often exhausting. Worth trying for fans of stylish action games, but the random storytelling, gameplay shifts, and overwhelming presentation make it difficult for me to recommend personally.

[h1]💃🔫 “Completely ridiculous—and all the better for it.” 👠😈[/h1]

Bayonetta is the kind of game that knows exactly what it is and commits to it without hesitation. It's absurd, over-the-top, stylish, and unapologetically confident from the opening moments to the credits.

At its core is one of the best combat systems in the character action genre. Bayonetta controls beautifully, with responsive movement, satisfying combos, and a combat flow that rewards both experimentation and mastery. Dodging at the last second to trigger Witch Time never stops being satisfying, turning defensive play into an opportunity for devastating counterattacks.

What impressed me most is how approachable it feels while still offering tremendous depth. You can enjoy the game by learning the basics, but the combat system has enough complexity to keep skilled players chasing higher ranks and more stylish combos for dozens of hours.

The boss fights and set pieces are pure spectacle. The game constantly escalates its insanity, throwing increasingly absurd scenarios at you and somehow making them work. One moment you're fighting angels in a cathedral, and the next you're battling something that feels like it escaped from the imagination of someone who was told "make it bigger" fifty times in a row.

The story is entertaining, though it's often less important than the sheer energy of the presentation. Characters are memorable, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the entire game exudes personality.

The heavy sexualization won't be for everyone, and some of the game's older design quirks occasionally show their age. But beneath all of that is an incredibly polished action game that helped define the genre.

Bayonetta doesn't ask you to take it seriously. It asks you to enjoy the ride—and what a ride it is. 🌙✨

Let's start with the bad parts. Playing with mouse and keyboard, even if doable and still fun, is not something I'd recommend and even setting it up is it's own kind of torture, with the game not having any keybinds at first and not letting you save your settings (just press [HOME] in the controls settings and then it works fine). Even if my PC is objectively a potato without gaming optimized GPU drivers, the specs are way above what I need to run this game. Never the less, setting it up to run at stable 60 took me hours and I still failed. The, after restarting my PC, it ran smooth like butter with absolutely no issues. That happened over and over, meaning each day I started playing, the framerate dropped bellow 30, forcing me to quit out, restart my PC and only then was I allowed to play. The amount of cutscenes and the placement of checkpoints was a bit annoying at times, but not enough to take away from the overall experience.
Now the good parts. It's pretty much everything else. Incredible combat with satisfying combos and a decent enemy variety to put all of them into practice. The whole game felt like a comedy action movie, where you're the star of the show and the better you get, the flashier and more entertaining it is. The dialog is pretty good overall, mostly a little stupid in a good, very fitting way. The models and environments are very pleasant to look at, even with it's outdated graphics. The soundtrack is absolutely amazing, perfectly supporting the tone of the game and tying it all together. There's also a bunch of minigames, which do amazing work at breaking up the pace of the game without really ruining it, even if none of them are anywhere near the level of quality the rest of the game is, outside of how cinematic they can look.
This game is a timeless classic for many reasons other than the main characters ass. A must play for basically anyone who enjoys action or gameplay that flashes out your own mechanical skills.
